6.244.m:
Śaṅkara said:
Then Rāma enjoyed delightful royal pleasures with Vaidehī
for a thousand years, protecting the quarters on all sides.

All the people of the inner apartments and also the subjects of the provinces
continually blamed Vaidehī, who had resided in the rākṣasa's house.

And from fear of public reproach, Rāma, the subduer of enemies,
manifesting human duty, [banished] the pregnant daughter of the king.

In the sacred hermitage of Vālmīki, on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the great forest,
the glorious one abandoned the pregnant woman amid the assembly of sages.

Dependent on her husband, she dwelt in the sage’s residence,
honored by the sages' wives and protected by the sage Vālmīki.

There she gave birth to twin sons, Kuśa and Lava by name;
and there they were initiated by the sage and grew up.

Rāma also, together with his brothers, ruled the earth,
endowed with restraints and other virtues, shunning all pleasures.

Constantly worshiping Viṣṇu, the beginningless and endless Hari,
ever dedicated to celibacy, the king ruled the earth.

Śatrughna, having slain Lavaṇa, ruled Mathurā,
built by the gods, together with his two sons, the righteous Rāghava.

Bharata, having slain the gandharvas on both banks of the Sindhu,
established his two mighty sons in that land.

And Lakṣmaṇa, having slain the Madras in the western Madra country,
and having consecrated his two heroic, mighty sons,

returned again to Ayodhyā and touched Rāma's feet.
A brāhmaṇa's dead boy, who had succumbed to death,

the descendant of Kakutstha brought back to life, after slaying a śūdra ascetic.
Then, on the bank of the Gautamī at Naimiṣa, in an assembly of people,

the Rāghava, slayer of enemy heroes, performed a horse sacrifice;
having fashioned a golden image of Jānakī, the mighty one [sacrificed] with her.

The Rāghava, knower of the supreme truth, performed sacrifices abundantly;
the lord [performed] ten thousand horse sacrifices and Vājapeya rites,

the Agniṣṭoma, the Viśvajit, the cow sacrifice, and a hundred sacrifices;
he performed various sacrifices completed with sacrificial gifts.

In the meantime, the ascetic of great austerity, Vālmīki,
bringing Sītā there, spoke these words to the descendant of Kakutstha:

Vālmīki said:
"O Rāma of virtuous vows, you ought not to abandon the sinless Maithilī today.
She is pure and faithful, like the splendor of the sun.
She has no devotion other than to you, O descendant of Kakutstha; why was she abandoned by you, O sinless one?"

Rāma said:
"O brāhmaṇa, from your words I know that the Maithilī is sinless today.
Formerly the faithful woman was carried off by Rāvaṇa in the solitary Daṇḍaka [forest].

Having slain him in battle, having received Sītā pure from the mouth of fire,
I returned again to Ayodhyā, taking Sītā in accordance with dharma.

A very great public reproach arose among the citizens;
out of fear of that, she of virtuous conduct was abandoned by me near you.

Therefore, for the satisfaction of the public, Sītā, devoted to me,
ought to offer proof before the kings and great seers."

Maheśvara said:
Being spoken to thus in the assembly of sages and kings,
the chaste goddess Sītā gave proof that astonished the world.

Showing to that world her undivided devotion to Rāma, the chaste
Sītā, with folded hands, spoke in the assembly of all the people:

Sītā said:
"Just as I think of no one other than the Rāghava even in my mind,
so may the goddess Earth give me an opening.

Just as the truth has been spoken by me, and I know none other than Rāma,
so may the Earth immediately come to her own daughter, Vaidehī."

Maheśvara said:
Then, carrying a jewel-inlaid throne on his back, the lord of birds [emerged]
from the netherworld, the hero recognizing his mother at that time.

Then the goddess Earth, taking the Maithilī by the hands
and greeting her with welcome, seated her upon the throne.

Seeing Sītā arrived, the hosts of gods in the sky
showered an unbroken, divine rain of flowers upon Sītā.

And she, the eternal one, being worshiped by divine apsarases,
mounted the son of Vinatā and went by that path to heaven.

Surrounded on the eastern side by hosts of maidservants, the sovereign of the world
reached the supreme, eternal abode accessible to yogins.

Seeing her entered into the netherworld, all the mortals
cried out loudly together: "Excellent! Excellent is Sītā!"

Overwhelmed with sorrow, Rāma took both sons
and entered Sāketa together with the sages and the foremost kings.

Then, after a great span of time, the mothers of strict vows
reached the fate appointed by time and went to their husband's heaven.

For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
the Rāghava of strict vows ruled the kingdom in accordance with dharma.

Then, after some time, Time arrived in the form of an ascetic
at the dwelling of the Rāghava and spoke these words:

Time said:
"Rāma, Rāma of mighty arms, I have been sent by the Creator.
Listen, O best of the Raghus, to what I say, O wise one.

Our conversation must be held strictly in private;
whoever enters between us shall surely be put to death."

Maheśvara said:
Consenting, "So be it," lotus-eyed Rāma
placed the son of Sumitrā at the door, and Time spoke his words;
Vaivasvata spoke these words to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha:

Time said:
"Listen, Rāma, to what took place as the cause of my coming:
'For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,

I shall dwell in the world of mortals, having slain the two foremost rākṣasas.'
Thus addressed by the hosts of gods, you descended to the surface of the earth.
Therefore, the time has come for you to go to heaven; / may all the gods indeed have their master today through you, O sinless one."
Maheśvara said: / "So be it," the Kakutstha Rāma replied to the great sage. / In the meantime, Durvāsas, rich in great penance,
approached the palace gate and spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa. / Durvāsas said: / "Go quickly and announce me to the Kakutstha, O prince!"
Maheśvara said: / Lakṣmaṇa said to him: "He is in seclusion, O twice-born." / Then, overcome with rage, the best of sages spoke to him:

Durvāsas said: / "I shall pronounce a curse if you do not bring me before Rāma, the Kakutstha!" / Maheśvara said: / Out of fear of that curse, he announced the twice-born to Rāghava. / Right then and there, Time, who brings terror to all beings, disappeared.
The king honored the sage Durvāsas who had arrived. / Knowing the solemn vow made by his elder brother, the best of the Raghus,
Lakṣmaṇa abandoned his human form in the waters of the Sarayū. / Relinquishing the human form, he entered his own body.
Endowed with a thousand hoods, brilliant as ten million moons, / wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrant pastes,
surrounded by thousands of serpent maidens, fully adorned, / he ascended a celestial chariot and went to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Learning the entire destination of Lakṣmaṇa, the best of the Raghus, / the Kakutstha himself also desired to go to heaven.
Having consecrated his two sons, Kuśa and Lava, the Kakutstha, / dividing chariots, elephants, horses, and wealth, gave [them] to the two.
The best of the Raghus established Kuśa in Kuśavatī / and Lava likewise in Śaravatī, righteously upon their kingdoms.
Learning the intention of Rāma, who knew the Self, / all the monkeys and the immensely powerful rākṣasas came.
Vibhīṣaṇa, then Sugrīva, Jāmbavat, the son of the Wind, / Nīla, Nala, Suṣeṇa, and Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas;
and the magnanimous Śatrughna, having consecrated his two heroic sons— / all these arrived at Ayodhyā, which was protected by Rāma.
Bowing to that great soul with folded hands, they spoke. / The monkeys and the others said: / "Knowing you are prepared to go to heaven, O best of the Raghus,
we all have come to follow you. / We cannot live for a moment without you, O Lord! / Therefore, O large-eyed one, let us go with you to the abode of the gods!"
Maheśvara said: / Addressed thus by them, the Kakutstha then said, "Very well." / Then the one of great splendor said to Vibhīṣaṇa, the king of the rākṣasas:

Rāma said: / "Rule the kingdom righteously; do not make my solemn vow futile. / As long as the moon and the sun remain, and as long as the earth endures, / so long take delight, well pleased; at the appointed time, go to my abode."

Maheśvara said: / Having spoken thus, that Kakutstha, the lotus-eyed Rāma, / with deep affection gave him the gentle eternal Viṣṇu, / his own form reclining at Śrīraṅga, the ancestral deity of the Ikṣvāku dynasty. / Then Rāghava, slayer of foes, spoke to Hanumat:
Rāma said: / "As long as stories about me circulate in the world, O lord of monkeys, / so long remain on earth; at the appointed time, come to me, O you of noble vows."

Maheśvara said: / Having spoken thus to him, the Kakutstha then said to Jāmbavat: / Rāma said: / "When the Dvāpara age arrives, I will be born on earth again / in the lineage of the Yadus for the destruction of the earth's burden.
I myself will fight a duel there, O best of bears."
Maheśvara said: / Having spoken thus to him, the Kakutstha, Rāma of mighty strength, / spoke with these words to all those bears and monkeys: "Come!"
The ministers, the townsmen, and Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, / resolute in following Rāghava, gathered together.
Then, clad in white garments, practicing celibacy, he set forth supreme; / taking kuśa grass in his two hands, absorbed [in contemplation], he set forth supreme.
At Rāma's right side went Ramā, holding a lotus in her hand; / likewise goddess Dharaṇī went on his other [side].
The Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, the Purāṇas along with the legendary histories on every side, / the [om-]sound, the vaṣaṭ-call, the world-purifying Sāvitrī,
and then the missiles and weapons, beginning with the bow, O Pārvatī, / all followed Rāma in human forms.
Bharata, Śatrughna, and all the city dwellers, / accompanied by their wives, sons, and attendants, followed the Kakutstha.
The ministers, the groups of servants, the attendants, and the townsmen, / as well as the monkeys and the bears together with Sugrīva,
along with their wives and sons, followed the wise Kakutstha. / Beasts, birds, and all the stationary and moving beings,
the best of men nearby, followed the great soul. / And those who beheld the Kakutstha, the Lord walking upon his path,
followed Rāma in that manner; not one turned back. / Then, having traveled three yojanas to the river that flowed toward the west,
he entered the Sarayū of sacred waters along with his followers. / Then Grandfather Brahmā, surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
along with the sages, praised the tiger of the Raghus with imperishable words, / and addressed the Kakutstha who had entered the waters of the Sarayū:
Brahmā said: / "Come, O Viṣṇu, hail to you! By good fortune have you arrived, O giver of honor! / Together with your brothers, who resemble gods, enter your own body,
that eternal form of Viṣṇu, of great splendor, possessing divine appearance! / For you are the refuge of the world, O God; yet some do not know you.
Enter, O lord, whatever body you wish, O one of great splendor, / you who are unthinkable, the great soul, imperishable, containing everything!"
Maheśvara said: / While that place was filled with sunbeams and showered with rains of flowers, / relinquishing his human form, he indeed entered his own body.
Both Śatrughna and Bharata, endowed with celestial splendor, / then [entered] his two parts, the conch and the discus, through that great soul.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, bow, and lotus in his four hands, / endowed with celestial ornaments, anointed with divine fragrant pastes,
wearing divine yellow garments, with eyes like lotus petals, / youthful, tender, with gentle limbs, radiant with delicate bodily parts,
with smooth, dark, curly locks, marked with auspicious signs, / dark as fresh dūrvā sprouts, his face resembling the full moon,
accompanied by the two goddesses, the glorious Lord ascended the celestial chariot / and sat upon the divine throne beneath the wishing tree,
the one of great splendor, praised by all the gods. / And the bears, monkeys, and humans who had followed Rāghava,
merely touching the waters of the Sarayū, abandoned their lives happily; / through Rāma's grace, they all assumed auspicious, celestial forms.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, possessing divine auspicious luster, / countless embodied beings ascended that celestial chariot there.
Surrounded by all, the glorious, lotus-eyed Rāma, / worshipped by hosts of gods and siddhas and by great-souled sages,
the all-pervading Lord returned to his own eternal, celestial, imperishable abode. / Whoever recites the story of Rāma, a verse or even half a verse,
Or if one hears it with devotion, or remembers it, O fair-faced lady, / from sins accumulated over ten million births, whether committed knowingly or in ignorance,
a person is freed and reaches the world of Viṣṇu, accessible only to yogins, / without any difficulty, along with their sons, wife, and kinsmen.

Thus has the great deeds of Rāma been related to you, O goddess. / Blessed am I on your account, O goddess, through the chanting of Rāmacandra's deeds! / What else do you wish to hear, O fair-faced lady? That I shall relate."

6.245.m: The venerable Pārvatī said: / "Well indeed have the deeds of the Lord of Raghu's line been related by you, O omnipresent Lord! / Hearing them, I am blessed, O Lord of gods, by your grace, O Great Lord.
The great deeds of this Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, / I desire to hear, O Lord of gods—the deeds that remove all sins."
Rudra said: / "Listen, O goddess! I shall proclaim the deeds of this great-souled Kṛṣṇa, / of Vāsudeva, which grant all fruits to mortals.
In the lineage of the Yadus, O goddess, was born Vasudeva, / the son of Devamīḍha, foremost among all knowers of dharma.
Devaka's daughter, Devakī, endowed with divine complexion, / that prince married according to the prescribed rites in Mathurā.
Ugrasena's son was Kaṃsa, heroic and endowed with great strength. / He drove the excellent chariot of the two as their charioteer.
As they were proceeding thus along the delightful and auspicious road, / a bodiless voice in the sky spoke with a deep sound:
The Voice from the Sky said: / 'Her eighth conception, O Kaṃsa, shall take away your life!'
Rudra said: / Hearing that, Kaṃsa began at once to slay his sister. / Vasudeva, using his own wits, spoke to him who was exceedingly agitated:
Vasudeva said: / "According to dharma, your sister must not be slain by you, O fortunate one! / Slay only the embryos as soon as they are born, O mighty king!"
Rudra said: / Saying 'So be it,' Kaṃsa then confined Vasudeva / and Devakī in his own delightful palace and kept them supplied with every enjoyment.
Meanwhile, O goddess, oppressed by the burden of sinners, / the goddess Earth went swiftly into the presence of Brahmā.
Having approached Brahmā, the Supreme Lord and master of the worlds, / Earth, the supporter of the realm, spoke with a deep voice:
Earth said: / "O Prajāpati, I am not able to uphold these worlds, O Lord! / Wicked-acting rākṣasas are settled upon me, O you of noble vows!
They are destroying all the dharmas of the world, full of great might; / all men, having the luster of adharma, are bewildered by sin.
Not even the slightest trace of dharma is seen in this world. / By dharma alone, O Lord, by truth, purity, and restraint, was I upheld; / therefore, I cannot bear a world born of adharma."
Rudra said: / Having spoken thus, the goddess Earth disappeared right there. / Then all the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā and Rudra,

reached the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk to find the Lord of the universe, / and together with the great ascetics and sages praised him with divine hymns. / Then, being pleased, the Lord spoke to all those foremost sages:
The Blessed Lord said: / "Hail, O hosts of gods! For what purpose have you all come here?" / Rudra said: / Then the Grandfather [Brahmā] spoke to Janārdana, the God of gods:
Brahmā said: / "O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, the earth is oppressed by a burden! / Many unassailable rākṣasas have arisen in the world:
Jarāsandha, Kaṃsa, Pralamba, Dhenuka, and others, / wicked-souled ones, are harassing all the eternal worlds.
You ought to relieve the burden of the earth here!" / Rudra said: / Thus addressed by Brahmā the Supreme Lord, / Hṛṣīkeśa, the imperishable Lord of the earth, spoke with a deep voice:
The Blessed Lord said: / "Descending then into this world in the lineage of the Yadus, O gods, / I shall remove the heavy burden of the earth, O mighty ones!"
Rudra said: / Having been told this, all the gods bowed down to Janārdana, / reached their respective worlds, and meditated upon the Supreme Lord. / Then the Supreme Lord spoke to Nārāyaṇī Māyā:
The Blessed Lord said: / "Bring the six sons of Hiraṇyākṣa to the surface of the earth, / and place them in the womb of Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva.
The seventh to enter here is a portion of Ananta; do not delay: / transfer him to her co-wife, Rohiṇī, O fair-faced lady!
Then, as the eighth, a portion of mine will be born in Devakī. / In Yaśodā, the wife of Nandagopa, however, you, eternal one,

constituting my portion as the Great Slumber, having gone to the great Vindhya mountain, / and there being worshipped by the gods headed by Indra, / must slay the daityas of great valor, headed by the demon Śumbha."
Rudra said: / Saying 'So be it,' Mahāmāyā then / introduced the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa in turn into Devakī as six embryos.
As soon as they were born, Kaṃsa of great might slew them. / Then the seventh embryo, prompted by the portion of Ananta,
she transferred to Rohiṇī while the embryo was growing. / From being dragged from the womb into her, the imperishable Saṃkarṣaṇa was born.
On the dark eighth day, under the constellation Rohiṇī in the month of Bhādrapada, at an auspicious dawn, / Rohiṇī gave birth to her son, the mighty Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Hari entered the womb of Devakī. / Seeing that she had conceived, Kaṃsa was stricken with fear.
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, / praised Devakī right there, situated in their aerial chariots in the vault of heaven.
Then, in the tenth month, in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O Pārvatī, / on the eighth day at midnight, Janārdana was born from her:
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with wide eyes like lotus leaves, / four-armed, with lovely limbs, adorned with divine ornaments,
his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, decorated with a forest garland— / this eternal Vāsudeva was born to Vasudeva.
Beholding that Lord of the universe, Kṛṣṇa, Ānakadundubhi, / joining his hands in reverence and bowing to him who embodies the universe, spoke:
Vasudeva said: / "You are born to me, O Lord of the universe, O wish-fulfilling tree of devotees, O Lord! / You alone are the beginningless Puruṣottama of all gods.
You are the unthinkable, the Great Being, the eternal one meditated upon by yogins, / who have assumed the state of being my son on earth, O upholder of the earth!
Seeing this wondrous divine form, O Puruṣottama, / the wicked-acting dānavas of great majesty will not tolerate it."
Rudra said: / Thus implored and praised by him, the eternal Padmanābha / withdrew that form endowed with four arms.
He shone forth in human manner with two arms. / And whatever bodyguards, dānavas, were stationed there,
they too were deluded by his Māyā and enveloped in darkness. / In the meantime, taking the divine child, Ānakadundubhi
departed swiftly from the city, praised by all the gods. / While the clouds were pouring rain, the mighty King of Serpents [Śeṣa]
covering the god with his thousand hoods, followed devotedly. / The two city-gate panels opened then at the touch of his feet,
bursting apart and wide open, while those standing there were completely deluded. / The Yamunā, a full-flowing river, for the great-souled one's
entrance, brought its water down to knee-depth only. / Crossing the Yamunā, the best of the Yadus then went to Vraja, situated on its bank,
and entered while being praised by the thirty gods. / There, in that auspicious cow-pen, the wife of Nanda had given birth,
deluded indeed by Māyā, deep asleep and enveloped in darkness. / Placing the god upon her bed, that Yādava
took up that girl and went back to Mathurā again. / Giving that child to his wife, he then sat down, completely composed.
Having gone to Devakī's bed, she wept due to her childish nature. / Hearing the child's cry, the bodyguards of that house
reported Devakī's auspicious delivery to Kaṃsa. / Kaṃsa arrived swiftly and then seized the baby girl.
And he dashed her onto the surface of a stone, but she swiftly stood in the sky. / Placing her foot on his head, she stood with a radiant face,
and the eight-armed goddess said then to the foremost of demons: / The Goddess said: / "What [is gained] by tossing me, foolish one? The one who will kill you has been born!
He who is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the whole world, the Lord, / has appeared in this world; he will take away your life."
Rudra said: / Having spoken thus, suddenly filling the sky with her splendor, the goddess / went to the Himālaya, being praised by the gods and Gandharvas.
Kaṃsa, his mind then agitated, summoned his demons— / Pralamba, Cāṇūra, and the rest—and, afflicted with fear, said:
Kaṃsa said: / "Out of fear of us, the hosts of gods approached the Ocean of Milk / and reported everything to Hari concerning the destruction of the demons.
Hearing their words, the supporter of the earth, the imperishable one, / has indeed been born on the earth in human form.
Therefore, today, all of you shapeshifting demons, / without hesitation kill all children who possess excessive strength!"
Rudra said: / Having ordered thus, Kaṃsa then consoled Vasudeva and Devakī, / released them, and entered the interior of his own palace. / Vasudeva then went to the incomparable Vraja of Nanda.
Honored there by him, having placed his son [there] with joy, / the delighter of the Yadus spoke to Yaśodā, that wife of Nanda:
Vasudeva said: / "Auspicious lady, this son of mine, born from Rohiṇī's womb, / who has come here out of fear of Kaṃsa, protect him like your own son!"
Rudra said: / "So be it," said Nanda's slender wife of firm vows then; / having obtained the twin sons, she reared them filled with joy.
Having placed his son in the home of the cowherd Nanda, / the Yādava, reassured, quickly departed for Mathurā, ruled by Kaṃsa.
Then, on an auspicious day, Garga, prompted by Vasudeva, / went to the cowherd Nanda's Vraja; the twice-born was honored by those dwelling there.
Having performed the birth rites of the Lord in Gokula according to rule, / he also gave divine names there to the two sons of Vasudeva.
The twice-born gave the names Saṃkarṣaṇa, Rauhiṇeya, Balabhadra of great strength, / Rāma, and others, to the elder brother.
Śrīdhara, Śrīkara, the glorious, Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Lord of the Universe, / Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, and so forth, to the younger brother;
"They will become known in this world as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa." / Having spoken thus, the best of the twice-born, having honored the ancestors and the deities,
and being honored by the cowherds, returned to Mathurā again. / Sent by Kaṃsa in the night, Pūtanā, the slayer of children,
gave her breast smeared with poison to Kṛṣṇa of boundless splendor. / But Kṛṣṇa, recognizing the demoness, drank the breast firmly and deeply,
along with the life-breaths of the demoness, that bull of the Yadus of great splendor. / Her limbs suddenly collapsing, the bonds of her sinews severed,
trembling, making a great sound, she fell and died. / And by her immense noise the vault of the sky was filled.
Terrified, all the cowherds then, seeing her fallen to the ground / and Kṛṣṇa playing upon the vast chest of the demoness,
greatly anxious then, quickly took up the child; / then, out of fear of demons, [sprinkling] cow dung upon his head,
they wiped his face with the tail of a cow. / The cowherd Nanda, having approached and taken up the son, O beautiful lady,
performed a cleansing on all his limbs with the names of the Lord. / Having removed that dark and dreadful [demoness] outside the cow-pasture,
the cowherd groups, terrified there in the cow-pasture, burned her. / Once, lying down beneath a cart, the blessed Lord Hari,
stretching out his two feet there, wept, Madhusūdana. / By the kick of his foot, the cart was overturned.
Its pots and jars smashed, it truly fell upside down. / Then the cowherd women and cowherds, seeing that great cart,
went into the greatest astonishment, wondering in doubt, "What is this?" / And Yaśodā, astonished, quickly took up the child.
In only a short time, those two boys, the best of the Yadus, / growing and nourished by the drinking of Yaśodā's breast-milk,
shone brightly, crawling on their knees and on their hands. / An illusory demon disguised as a young boy was made [to go] there;
setting out to kill Kṛṣṇa, he moved about upon the surface of the earth. / Recognizing that demon, Kṛṣṇa struck him down with his palm.
In his demonic form itself he fell down and died. / Thereupon Madhusūdana wandered through the entire cow-pasture,
and swiftly stole fresh butter in house after house of the cowherd women. / Then Yaśodā, angered, having bound Kṛṣṇa
at his waist with a cord to a wooden mortar, set out to sell dairy products and other goods. / Then Kṛṣṇa, dragging along, bound with the cord to the mortar,
the supporter of the earth, went between the twin Arjuna trees. / With the mortar, Govinda caused the two trees to fall down.
With broken trunks they crashed onto the surface of the earth with a loud sound. / At that immense sound, [the cowherds] of great might arrived there.
The elder cowherds, seeing [it] then, went into extreme astonishment. / Yaśodā too, greatly anxious, untied the supporter of the earth,
and, taking up the astonished, great-souled one, gave him her breast. / When the Lord of the Universe was bound by his mother with a cord,
at that time he was called "Dāmodara" by all the great seers. / The twin Arjuna trees, liberated, attained the state of Kinnaras.
Then all the elder cowherds, led by the cowherd Nanda, / recognizing this great portent, went to another place.
In delightful Vṛndāvana, on the auspicious bank of the Yamunā, / they made a charming dwelling for the cows and for the cowherd folk.
There, growing up, those two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, possessing great strength / and joined by the calf-herders, tended the calves then.
As Kṛṣṇa was in the midst of the calves, a great Asura named Baka, / in the form of a heron, undertook here to kill that best of Yadus.
Seeing him, Vāsudeva too effortlessly picked up a clod of earth / and struck him at the tip of his wing; the great Asura fell to the earth.
Then, after a few days, while tending the calves in the forest, / the two fell fast asleep in the shade of a rose-apple tree on soft sprouts.
In the meantime, the god Brahmā, surrounded by the hosts of gods, / arrived to see Kṛṣṇa and saw the two best of the Yadus asleep.
Stealing the calves and the cowherd children, he went back to heaven. / The two of them woke up and saw that the children and calves had vanished.
"Where have the calves and the cowherd boys gone?" they wondered, astonished. / Knowing then that it was an act performed by Prajāpati,
the eternal Madhusūdana created the children and calves just as they were, / so swiftly and of the same form.
The Lord, the protector of the worlds, created the calves and cowherds. / Seeing them at evening time, the cows and their mothers,
approached their respective calves and behaved just as before. / In this way, when a year's time had passed there for the great-souled one,
Prajāpati gave back to him the calves together with the boys. / Folding his hands in reverence, circumambulating and bowing down, / out of fear Brahmā, the lord of the three worlds, spoke to Govinda:
Brahmā said: / "Salutations, salutations to you, the Self of all, whose nature is the knowledge of truth, / whose nature is eternal bliss, the beloved Self, the Great-souled One!
Minute, vast, of exceedingly gross form, all-pervading, imperishable, / whose form has no beginning, middle, or end, whose nature is the Self—salutations to you!
To the one composed of eternal knowledge, strength, lordship, vigor, and splendor, / the great power, possessing the form of the complete six attributes, salutations to you!
You are the Veda-Puruṣa, O Brahman, and the Mahā-Puruṣa; / you are the Śarīra-Puruṣa and the Chandaḥ-Puruṣa.
You are the four Puruṣas, the ancient Puruṣottama. / O Brahman, your divine manifestations are earth, fire, wind, and the rest.
Earth and fire arose from your speech, O Lord of the universe; / the atmosphere and wind were created from your breath, O all-pervading Lord.
By your eye the sky and the sun were created, O imperishable one; / and the directions and the moon were created by your ear, O sinless one.
The flowing of the waters and Varuṇa [arose] from your mind, O Great Lord. / What shines forth as Brahman in the great Mīmāṃsā that is spoken of,
and likewise in the sacrifices, this very one is in the Mahāvrata; / in the song of the Chāndogas, in the sky is this, in heaven is this, it is wind itself.
This very one is space, this very one is in the plants likewise; / and in all the lunar mansions, in the planets is this, and in the sun.
Thus, in the beings likewise, Śruti proclaims [it] to be Brahman. / That very supreme Brahman is known all around as the immortal.
Golden, imperishable, sacrifice, pure, and dwelling in the pure— / these are Vedic designations, and nowhere do they belong [solely] to another.
Consisting of sight, hearing, sacred meter, and mind, / consisting of speech—thus Śruti praises the supreme Self, the highest Lord.
"Thus you are the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, O lotus-eyed one; / I am unable to praise you, who have gone beyond all the Vedāntas."
This was a great offense of mine: the theft of the calves performed by me. / Let that be forgiven, O Lord, who are affectionate to those seeking refuge!"
Maheśvara said: / Having thus praised Hari, the Creator, bowing down again and again / and returning the calves to him, departed to his own abode.
Holding Hari in the form of a child always in his heart, O goddess, Brahmā, / of great asceticism, lived together with the gods, glad and thriving.
The calves created by Kṛṣṇa, the previous calves, and the boys / attained unity right there while the heaven-dwellers watched.
Kṛṣṇa went with the keepers of the calves to Nanda's cow-pasture. / Then, after several days had passed, the bull among the Yadus, with the cowherds,
approached the pool of the Kālindī. Acyuta [confronted] the very venomous, / mighty serpent king dwelling there, who had a thousand heads.
Crushing the thousand hoods effortlessly with a single foot, / Madhusūdana brought him into mortal danger.
That Kāliya, regaining consciousness, went to him alone for refuge. / Then the Blessed Kṛṣṇa protected the serpent, whose poison was abandoned.
Marking him on the heads with his own footprint as he was terrified of Vainateya, / the bull among the Yadus expelled him from the pool of the Kālindī.
Leaving that pool quickly together with his children and wives, / Kāliya bowed to Govinda and then departed.
The trees standing on its banks that had formerly been scorched by poison, / when looked upon by Kṛṣṇa, quickly bore fruit and flowers.
Then in time Madhusūdana, reaching childhood, / protected the herd of cattle, the Lord consisting of all the gods.
With cowherd boys of the same age as himself, the best of the Yadus / wandered in the charming Vṛndāvana together with Rāma.
There, having killed a terrible great demon in the form of a serpent, / casting aside the huge-bodied one with the weight of Meru and Mandara,

he reached Dhenuka's forest, a thicket of palmyra and date-palms. / Entering that lovely, fruit-bearing forest, a palmyra thicket, / [he encountered] Dhenuka, mountain-sized, who always held the form of an ass.
Seizing him by the two feet and lifting him up, he struck him down against a palmyra tree. / Right at that moment the cowherds made merry after his demise.
Departing swiftly from that forest, they came to the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree; / there they played with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in childish sport.
A rākṣasa named Pralamba arrived there in the guise of a cowherd. / Putting Rāma on his back, he quickly went into the sky.
Recognizing him as a rākṣasa, Rāma struck him on the head with his fist / in anger; his limbs convulsing, he fell from there.
In the very form of a rākṣasa, roaring a terrifying roar, / with shattered head and body, he died there, drenched in blood.
Then, at evening time, in the cowherd station, the son of Nanda / dwelt, sporting with the cowherd girls in the glow of the white water-lilies.
A lord of daityas named Ariṣṭa, going there in the form of a bull, / arrived to kill Kṛṣṇa and roared with a mighty roar.
Seeing him, all the cowherds fled, afflicted with fear. / Kṛṣṇa too, seeing that fierce lord of the danujas arrive,
uprooted a palmyra tree and crushed him between the horns. / He, with his head and horns broken, vomiting much blood,
fell with terrible speed, roaring, and gave up his life. / Having thus killed that huge-bodied lord of the danujas, Ariṣṭa,
and calling the cowherd boys, he dwelt right there in the cowherd settlement. / Then, after several days, a great demon named Keśin,
in the form of a horse, came to the settlement to kill Govinda. / Going to the charming cowherd settlement, he then neighed loudly.
By that great sound, the three worlds were filled. / All the hosts of gods were frightened, suspecting the end of an age.
All the cowherd men and women stationed there were bewildered and distressed; / but having regained consciousness, they all fled in every direction.
The cowherd women took refuge with Kṛṣṇa and cried, "Save us!" / "Do not fear! Do not fear!" said the one affectionate to devotees.
Having consoled them, the younger brother of Vāsava quickly / struck that demon on the head with his fist, as if in sport.
His teeth and eyes shattered, he bellowed with a great noise. / Lifting a huge rock, [Kṛṣṇa] brought it down upon his body.
With all his limbs crushed, roaring a terrifying cry, / that great demon suddenly fell to the ground and died.
Seeing Keśin slain, the hosts of gods in heaven released / great showers of flowers and exclaimed, "Well done! Well done!"
Having thus slain those mighty Daityas during his childhood, / Hari rejoiced in happiness, together with Balarāma.
Dark as a blue lotus petal, with eyes resembling lotus leaves, / wearing yellow garments, wearing a garland, adorned with a forest garland,
his chest shining with the Kaustubha gem, smeared with ointment and wearing colorful wreaths, / endowed with wondrous ornaments, resplendent with a pair of earrings,
adorned with a tulasī garland, marked with a musk tilaka, / having hair styled into very glossy, black, curly locks,
crowned with an ornament of peacock feathers bound with various flowers, / with palms and soles of his feet resembling red lotuses, and lovely lips,
his face possessing creeper-like eyebrows like the mark on the cool-rayed moon in the midst of a fortnight, / resplendent with necklaces, anklets, armlets, and a pair of bracelets—
in the greatly delightful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fruits and flowers, / making his charming flute resound, there stayed the delight of the Yadus.
Seeing Acyuta, whose beauty surpassed ten million Kamas, / all the cowherd women were afflicted by the arrow of Manmatha.
Formerly, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, / upon seeing Rāma, Hari, desired to enjoy his beautiful form.
They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula; / having reached Hari through desire, they were released from the ocean of worldly existence.
Just as the Daityas, confronting Madhusūdana in anger alone, / reached death in battle and, having been slain, obtained liberation—
desire and anger are indeed the cause of hell for men in the world; / [yet] approaching Hari through their inner feelings, the cowherd women and the enemies of the gods attained liberation.
Those who worship Janārdana out of desire, fear, or enmity / reach Vaikuṇṭha—what then of those [worshiping] through the yoga of devotion?
Hearing the sound of his flute in the night, the cowherd women / all rose from their beds, with their garments and hair disheveled.
Leaving their husbands, sons, and daughters-in-law, abandoning shame and their family, / afflicted by the arrows of Kama, they approached the Lord of the Universe.
All the cowherd women, having come together, embraced Keśava with their arms, / and the fair ladies enjoyed his lower lip as the immortals [enjoy] nectar.

6.245.s:
tābhiḥsarvābhirātmeśaḥ krīḍayāmāsagovraje
tenāpitāḥ striyaḥ sarvā remirenirbhayāvraje
6.245.d:
ताभिःसर्वाभिरात्मेशः क्रीडयामासगोव्रजे
तेनापिताः स्त्रियः सर्वा रेमिरेनिर्भयाव्रजे
6.245.m: With all of them the Lord of the self sported in the cow-station; / protected by him, all the women made love fearlessly in Vraja,
In this manner they delighted Keśava day after day / in delightful Vṛndāvana and on the sandbanks of the Kālindī.
Pārvatī said: / Having descended onto the earth for the purpose of preserving dharma, / how could Janārdana engage in approaching the wives of others?
Rudra said: / In one's own body and in others' limbs there is no distinction, O fair-faced one; / the entire universe is his limb; nothing here exists separately.
There is indeed no distinction of female and male for that supreme Puruṣa; / because of his inherent status as husband, and because the Lord of the Universe is the Lord of the self,
and through the power of that all-pervading Lord to remove sin, / no fault exists here, O blessed lady, for the God, the Supreme Self.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Having spoken thus to the daughter of the mountain, Rudra, the destroyer of Tripura, / began to narrate the rest of Kṛṣṇa's deeds.
Rudra said: / When autumn arrived, the cowherds, led by the cowherd Nanda, / began to perform a great festival for the Lord of the Thirty [Gods].
Preventing that festival of Śatakratu, the powerful Govinda / caused it to be performed instead for the king of mountains, Govardhana.
Then the thousand-eyed Indra, enraged, poured down a great rain / upon the cow-station of the cowherd Nanda continuously for seven nights.
Uprooting Govardhana, the great mountain, Janārdana / held it up playfully for the protection of the cows.
Reaching the shelter of that mountain, O virtuous lady, the cowherd men and women / lived in comfort, just as though they were inside a palace.
Then Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, frightened, with a bewildered mind, / stopped that rain and went to that Vraja of Nanda.
Kṛṣṇa too placed that great mountain back as it was before; / and all those cowherd elders, led by the cowherd Nanda,
worshiped Govinda and were filled with extreme wonder. / Then the god Śatakratu, having approached Madhusūdana, / praised him with folded hands in a voice faltering with joy:
Indra said: / Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one, omniscient Trivikrama! / Beyond the three guṇas, Lord of all, Self of the universe, praise be to you!
You are the sacrifice, you are the vaṣaṭ-call, you are the syllable Oṃ, the rite, the oblation; / you alone are the father and the mother of all the gods, O Keśava.
In the beginning you existed as Hiraṇyagarbha, the lord of what has come to be; / you alone are the one master, you are the golden Puruṣa.
You alone have supported this earth and the sky, O God; / you are the giver of the self, the giver of fruit, O Lord of the Universe!
That light of the Lord of the worlds has been obtained by the Thirty [Gods]; / immortality and death are your shadow, O eternal one.
To that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation, / from whom these snow-clad, golden [mountains] arose.
He whose tongue is the oceans, and whose arm is the wind, O Keśava, / whose directions and intermediate directions are these, O imperishable one—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation, / by whom, by you, the earth was mounted and caused to grow again.
By whom the heavenly realm was propped up, by you, O Brahman, O Maheśvara! / Clothed in the atmosphere of mist, all-pervading, imperishable—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation, / whom the two roaring realms, shining, of burning brilliance and endowed with virtues,
beheld with their mind, and necessarily Śrī at all times, / where the sun, having risen, shines in the highest abode—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation! / When the vast waters, the Janārdanas of the illusion of the Brahman of the universe,
bearing the embryo in this creation, producing [beings], destroying the flood of sins, / then arose the one imperishable, all-pervading spirit of the gods—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation! / Which waters in their greatness surveyed the capable Prajāpati,
bearing the sacrifice there in the beginning, producing the oblation, the Puruṣa; / who alone was the one supreme deity beyond the highest among the gods—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation! / May he not harm us, he who is the generator of the earth, the imperishable Puruṣa;
or who, true to dharma, generated the sky, the imperishable Lord; / and who generated the moon, the vast waters, and the whole world—
to that God, to you, we would offer worship with oblation! / All these beings in the universe came to be around you, O Lord;
O overseer of creatures born from you, the future and the past, O Acyuta! / We worship you, and whatever desires we have, let that be ours in sum.
May we become lords of the three [worlds] through your compassionate glance! / The Puruṣa named Golden, who has a golden beard and hair,
golden completely unto the tips of his nails, Savitṛ partaking of gold; / this all-pervading Brahman who is established within the sun—
we always meditate on that excellent, highest radiance of the divine Savitṛ, / which indeed illuminates our intellects.
Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one, Lord of Śrī, Lord of all, Keśava! / Known through the Vedānta, Lord of sacrifice, having the form of sacrifice, homage be to you!
Homage to you, Vāsudeva! Homage to you disguised as a cowherd! / From the destruction of all that, O God, an offense has been committed by me.

Therefore, forgive me, O Lord of the universe, ocean of compassion, highest of persons! / In a very short time, slay the unassailable Kaṃsa, / doing good for the gods and establishing the earth in peace."
Mahādeva said: / Having thus praised Govinda, Hari, the lord of all the gods, / anointed him with nectar, divine garments, and ornaments.
And having worshipped the lord of the gods, he went back to heaven. / The elder cowherds and the cowherd women, seeing Śatakratu there,
and being honoured by him, experienced incomparable joy. / Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, of great prowess, adorned with divine ornaments,
dwelt happily in the lovely cowherd station of Nanda. / In the meantime, O goddess, Nārada, the best of sages,
went swiftly to Mathurā and entered Kaṃsa's presence. / Honoured there by the king, seated upon an auspicious seat,
he related all the deeds of the bow-wielder [Kṛṣṇa]: / the undertaking of the deities, the birth of Keśava,
and how Vasudeva placed his son in the cowherd station; / the death of the rākṣasas, the banishment of the king of serpents,
the lifting of the best of mountains, and the arrival of Śatakratu. / Having reported everything completely to Kaṃsa,
he departed for the abode of Brahmā, honoured by that rākṣasa. / Kaṃsa, his mind deeply agitated, surrounded by his ministers,

deliberated with them concerning his own death. / There, to Akrūra, the foremost of the wise and devoted to righteousness, / the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas spoke words concerning his own welfare:
Kaṃsa said: / "Out of fear of me, all the gods, led by Śatakratu, / approached Viṣṇu and, stricken with fear, sought refuge.
Granting them fearlessness, the Blessed One, the source of beings, / Madhusūdana, was born in the womb of Devakī to kill me.
The wicked Vasudeva deceived me at night / and placed his son in the home of the utterly evil Nanda.
Though only a boy, difficult to overcome, he slew the great asuras; / he will undoubtedly be prepared to slay me as well.
He cannot be slain even by the gods and asuras together with Indra; / he must therefore be slain by a stratagem after being brought here by me.
With elephants wild with rut, with wrestlers, and with choice steeds, / by some means or another he can be slain right here.
Therefore, go to the cowherd station, O Yādava, / and bring Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, along with all the elder cowherds headed by Nandagopa, / here to enjoy the bow sacrifice, O best of the Yadus!"
Mahādeva said: / Saying "So be it," that best of Yadus, full of valour, mounted his chariot / and departed for lovely Gokula, eager to behold Kṛṣṇa.
That foremost of great devotees, Akrūra, full of humility, / beheld the untroubled Kṛṣṇa standing amidst the cows:
resembling a dark blue raincloud, adorned with every ornament, / with wide eyes like lotus petals, long-armed, free from affliction,
clad in yellow garments, handsome in every limb, / his chest radiant with the Kaustubha gem, adorned with jewelled earrings,
endowed with a garland of forest flowers and tulasī, with an ear-garland of wild blossoms; / seeing Janārdana there, surrounded by cowherd maidens,
his whole body bristling with joy, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, / that best of Yadus stepped down from his chariot and bowed low.
Approaching the cowherd with delight, circumambulating and bowing, / taking the two lotus feet that resemble red lotuses / and are marked with the thunderbolt and discus,
and placing them on his head, he bowed again and again. / Seeing the Lord, who resembles the peak of Kailāsa, clad in blue garments,
resembling the autumn full moon, adorned with strings of pearls, / that Yādava then bowed down to Balarāma.
Raising him up with joy and embracing those two heroes, the best of the Yadus, / the two heroes went home together with that Vṛṣṇi, Akrūra.
Nandagopa, seeing that best of Yadus arrived, / went to meet him, radiant with glory, and seated him on an excellent seat.
He worshipped him properly with water for reception and for the feet, with joy, / and worshipped him with devotion, presenting divine garments and offerings.
Akrūra, the Yādava, presented garments and ornaments / to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and to Nandagopa and Yaśodā.
Having inquired about their welfare, sitting untroubled on a seat of kuśa grass, / the wise man, being questioned about all royal affairs, spoke:
Akrūra said: / "This Kṛṣṇa of great splendour is imperishable Nārāyaṇa himself, / for the welfare of the gods and the protection of the virtuous,
for the removal of the earth's burden, for the establishment of righteousness, / and for the destruction of all daityas, beginning with Kaṃsa.
Implored by the hosts of gods and by great-souled sages, / he was born from the womb of Devakī at the deep of night in the rainy season.
Out of fear of Kaṃsa, Ānakadundubhi [Vasudeva] brought the Lord of gods, / Hari, that night and placed his son in your house.
At that very time, the renowned Yaśodā / gave birth to an auspicious-faced girl born from a portion of Māyā.
All this auspicious family of Vraja was bewitched by her. / Placing the best of Yadus, Kṛṣṇa, upon the bed of Yaśodā who had fainted,
and taking that girl, he went to his own house; / placing her on Devakī's bed, he went outside.
She then wept aloud as she lay on Devakī's bed. / Hearing that, Kaṃsa immediately seized the girl, O you of virtuous vows!

Swinging her around, the mighty one leaped up and dashed her on the surface of a rock. / Rising up, that girl, endowed with eight arms bearing weapons, / stood in the sky and spoke to Kaṃsa in anger with a deep voice:
The maiden said: / 'He who is the infinite Lord of all gods, the highest of persons, / has gone to the cowherd station for your slaughter, O lowest of Dānavas!'"
Akrūra said: / "Having spoken thus, that Mahāmāyā went to the Himavat mountain. / From then on, that wicked soul, his mind agitated by fear,
sent Dānavas for the slaughter of the great-souled one; / but though merely a child, all of them were slain in sport by this wise one.
The supreme lord performed exceedingly wondrous deeds: / the lifting of Govardhana and other feats, the banishment of the serpent king,
the visit of Mahendra, and the slaying of all the demons. / Having heard this recounted by the divine sage, exceedingly afflicted with fear,
bringing the mighty-armed Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who are difficult to conquer, from here, / he is resolved to kill them with great elephants wild with rut or with wrestlers.
He dispatched me here to bring Kṛṣṇa; / that wicked soul has imprisoned Vasudeva.
All this conduct of the utterly evil one has been recounted. / To enjoy the bow sacrifice, all of you dwellers of Vraja,
taking curd, clarified butter, and other offerings, should go tomorrow / into his presence, all cowherds accompanied by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Kaṃsa will surely be slain by Kṛṣṇa, there is no doubt; / therefore, casting aside fear, you must go at the king's command."
Īśvara said: / Having spoken thus, the very wise Akrūra fell silent. / Hearing his dreadful, hair-raising words,
all the elder cowherds, headed by Nandagopa, stricken with fear, / bewildered with grief, spoke in an ocean of great sorrow.
Having seen them there and comforted them, lotus-eyed Hari, the valiant one, spoke concerning the demon: 'You must have no fear.
Together with Rāma, joining with all of you, I shall depart for Mathurā to destroy this wicked Kaṃsa.
Having slain the wicked Kaṃsa there, the foremost of the Dānavas, and having slain all the demons, I shall protect the earth.
Therefore, cast off your grief and go to the city of Mathurā.' When they were spoken to thus by Hari, the cowherds headed by Nanda
embraced him repeatedly and smelled his head, considering the immeasurable deeds of the great-souled one.
And by Akrūra's words, all the cowherds were freed from pain. And with milk, curds, and ghee, pure and of various kinds,
cooked foods delightful to the heart, tasty and sweet, Yaśodā offered a plentiful, agreeable feast to Akrūra.
Together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and the best of cowherds headed by Nanda, with friends, children, and old men in the well-adorned house,
the best of the Yādavas enjoyed the food given by Yaśodā, which was agreeable, dispelled defilement, removed illness, and was auspicious.
Having fed him according to rule and given water for sipping, that woman of firm vows offered him betel with camphor.
When the sun had set, having performed his twilight devotion and having eaten the excellent rice cooked with milk together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
Akrūra then went to bed with those two. And in that excellent, charming house adorned with lamps,
on a smooth, multicolored couch adorned with various flowers, Hari Kṛṣṇa lay down like Nārāyaṇa on Śeṣa.
Beholding him, Akrūra suddenly was covered with tears of joy and horripilation; casting off sluggish sleep and perceiving the supreme blessing,
that foremost of devotees massaged the feet of Viṣṇu: 'To this extent is my life fruitful and well-lived!
This is sovereignty over the three worlds; this indeed is the highest happiness; this is kingship; this is righteousness; this is the supreme bliss of liberation!
These feet cannot be recollected in the mind by deities like Śiva and Brahmā, nor by the best of sages headed by Sanaka, nor by the great seers headed by Vasiṣṭha.
The pair of feet of that Lord of Śrī, radiant like autumn lotuses, / was touched by the two hands of Indirā Lakṣmī, [giving] supreme, boundless bliss.
By good fortune the auspicious pair of lotus feet of Viṣṇu has been attained by me!' Because of the weight of the bliss of Brahman, that night passed in an instant.
Then, at pure dawn, being praised by the foremost of the hosts of gods in heaven, Hari awoke from that bed.
Having sipped water according to rule, he together with the wise Rāma fell at his mother's feet and approved of the departure.
Raising them up, Yaśodā, overwhelmed with grief and joy, her face filled with tears, embraced her two sons with love.
That lady of firm vows gave her blessing to her two sons, and having embraced the two great heroes repeatedly, she sent them off.
Akrūra also, bowing down to Yaśodā, spoke with joined palms:
Akrūra said: 'I shall depart, O blessed lady; grant me your favor, O sinless one! This mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, having slain the very powerful Kaṃsa,
will become the king of the entire world, there is no doubt. Therefore, cast off sorrow and be happy, O woman of lovely face!'
The Lord said: Spoken to thus by her, Akrūra, the best of the Yadus, dismissed [by her], mounted his excellent chariot together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
He set out quickly for Mathurā, praised by groups of apsarases. All the cowherd elders, headed by the cowherd Nanda, followed him,
bringing curds, ghee, and various fruits once more. Seeing Hari departing from Gokula, the cowherd women
followed Madhusūdana who had gone forth seated on the chariot. Hari sent back all those cowherd women.
Their hearts tormented with sorrow, they lamented to the lotus-eyed one: 'Alas, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! O Govinda!' they cried repeatedly.
With eyes filled with tears, wretched and weeping, they remained there. Then Akrūra drove the divine chariot from the cow-settlement
toward Mathurā, that Yādava together with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. Having crossed the Yamunā quickly and halted the excellent chariot on the bank,
he stepped down from that chariot and proceeded to bathe there, and to perform his obligatory rites, diving into the auspicious water.
Reciting well the Aghamarṣaṇa [hymn] there, that foremost of devotees saw both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa endowed with auspiciousness in the water.
He beheld Rāma, resembling a crore of autumn moons, wearing blue garments, the lord, his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood, with the splendor of pearl ornaments,
having eyes like red lotuses, wearing a lotus garland as a crest; and [he beheld] Kṛṣṇa, resembling a dark blue rain-cloud,
wearing divine yellow garments, with wide lotus eyes, his limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood, adorned with various jewels.
Seeing them there, the best of the Yadus was filled with supreme wonder. Rising up, he saw the two of great strength there on the chariot.
Diving down again into that [water] while repeating the two-syllabled mantra of Hari, he saw Hari on the couch of Śeṣa in the ocean of nectar together with Ramā,
praised by Sanaka and the others, worshipped by all the gods. Having seen the god in that water, he was filled with supreme wonder; / then the best of the Yadus praised Hari, the all-pervading lord:
Akrūra said: 'Salutations to you whose self is Time, and who are without beginning or end! Salutations to the unmanifest; salutations to you who are free from alteration!
Salutations to the sustainer of creatures, salutations, salutations to the tiger among beings! Salutations to you, the supreme self, the controller of all beings!
To the changing and the unchanging, and to the directly perceivable spirit! Salutations to you, the maintainer of qualities, salutations, salutations to cosmic order!
To the supreme self, free from distinctions of space, time, and the like! Salutations to the infinite, salutations, salutations to Acyuta!
Salutations to Govinda, the lord of the triple Veda, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow! To Nārāyaṇa, the universal, salutations to you, Vāsudeva!
To Viṣṇu of manifold forms, salutations, salutations to the eternal one! To the lotus-eyed, the permanent, who bears the conch and the discus!
Whose splendor is graced with ornaments resembling a crore of rising suns! Salutations, salutations to Hari, the lord of all the worlds!
To the progenitor, the seed of all the worlds, the supreme self! Salutations, salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Kṛṣṇa, to Pradyumna!
To Aniruddha, the creator and the ordainer, the womb of the universe! To you of a thousand forms, with many heads, feet, and arms!
Of a thousand names, eternal, salutations, salutations to the Puruṣa! Salutations to you who recline on the serpent couch, having a gentle form!

Salutations to Keśava, and to the wearer of yellow garments, whose brilliance shines from friction in the embrace of Lakṣmī's firm breasts! / Salutations to Śrīdhara, to the Lord of Śrī, who has infinite forms!'
The Lord said: 'Whatever man, meditating upon the eternal god with devotion at the time of bathing, recites this hymn, is indeed freed from great sins.
Having attained the fruit of all holy places, he reaches union with Viṣṇu.' Having praised the god in the water in this way, that foremost of devotees
He worshipped [him] with water and fragrant flowers. / Having fulfilled his purpose, Akrūra then came out from the water of the Yamunā.
Approaching Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, full of auspiciousness, he bowed down. / Seeing him modest and astonished, Govinda, Hari, spoke to him:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / "What wonder did you see in that water, O Yādava?" / Īśvara said: / Akrūra then spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Yadus, who was full of great splendour:
Akrūra said: / "O Lord, master of the universe, for your omnipresent greatness, / what wonder is there, O Hṛṣīkeśa? Truly you alone are the entire universe!
You are the waters, you are the sky, the fire, you are the earth, and likewise the wind; / you are this entire fourfold world, immovable and moving.
Nothing exists apart from you, O Vāsudeva, as nectar [comes] from a cloud. / You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise the oblation.
You alone are the eternal, imperishable Lord of all the gods, / higher than what is caused or uncaused, beyond cause and effect.
To protect dharma, O Lord of the gods, you assume a body; / you have attained majesty in the forms of the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and others.
You alone, O all-pervading one, protect this entire world consisting of yourself."
Īśvara said: / Having praised Govinda thus and bowed to the lord of the worlds, / that best of the Yadus mounted his divine chariot along with the two of them.
Then, quickly reaching Mathurā, built by the gods, / he placed Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at the city gate and went to the inner palace.
Having announced their arrival to the king at that time, / he was honoured by the king and then entered his own house.
Then, at eventide, the mighty Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, / holding each other's hands, arrived in Mathurā.
Walking along the royal highway, the two great-souled best of the Yadus, / endowed with great valour, saw a washerman dyeing clothes.
He was clad in divine garments, on his way to the king’s house; the valiant Acyuta, / along with Rāma, asked him for those clothes.
The washerman did not give [them] to him then, out of anger; / standing there on the road, he spoke many harsh words.
The mighty Kṛṣṇa struck him with his palm alone; / he was slain right there on the road, vomiting much blood.
The two heroes, Rāma and Keśava, put on those lovely garments / along with their cowherd companions, as was suitable.
Reaching a garland-maker's house, they were seen and saluted by him; / being worshipped with fragrant, divine flowers, they were filled with joy.

Those two bulls among the Yadus granted him the boon he desired. / Returning again to the street, [they saw] a fair-faced woman approaching,

Seeing a hunchbacked woman, O two fortunate ones, holding a vessel of sandalwood paste, / a lady with a crooked back and limbs, [the two of them] begged her for fragrance.
Smiling, she then gave excellent sandalwood paste to the two of them. / Taking the divine sandalwood paste and anointing themselves as they pleased,
and having given her an exceedingly lovely form, they walked along the road, / gazed upon by women, tender and fair-faced.
The two great-souled ones entered the hall of sacrifice with their followers. / Seeing the divine bow worshipped there, Keśava
effortlessly seized it and then broke it, O Madhusūdana! / Hearing that bow being broken, Kaṃsa was deeply agitated.
Summoning the wrestlers, the charioteers, and the foremost leaders of the Daityas, / after consulting with his ministers, the bull of Daityas spoke to Cāṇūra:
Kaṃsa said: / "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa have arrived, the destroyers of all the Daityas. / In the morning, let them be killed in a wrestling match without hesitation.
By whatever means possible, those two who are arrogant with strength must be slain, / whether by elephants maddened with rut or diligently by the chief wrestlers."
Īśvara said: / Having commanded thus, the king, together with his younger brother and ministers, / quickly mounted to the top of his divine palace out of fear.
At the gates and on all the roads he stationed rutting elephants; / he stationed wrestlers and rut-maddened elephants on all sides.
Knowing all of that, Kṛṣṇa, along with the wise Rāma / and his followers, spent the night there in the house of sacrifice.
Then, when the night had passed and the pure dawn had arrived, / the two heroes, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, arose from sleep and performed their water rites.
Adorned and having eaten, eager to face the combat, / they went out from that house like two lions from a great cave.
Standing at the king’s gate was an elephant resembling the peak of the Himalaya mountain, / named Kuvalayāpīḍa, who increased Kaṃsa’s victories,
who crushed the pride of the divine elephants, gigantic, maddened with rut. / Seeing that great elephant, Keśava, like a lion,
seized its trunk with his hand alone, leapt up gracefully in play, / whirled it around, and then threw it onto the earth, the supporter of the earth.
With all its limbs crushed, roaring with a terrible sound, / that great elephant suddenly fell to the ground and died.
Having killed it, Rāma and Keśava tore out both tusks and took them; / they then entered the arena to wage battle with the wrestlers.
Seeing Govinda’s prowess, the Dānavas stationed there, / terrified, all fled and went to the king's inner palace.
Having firmly barred both door-leaves, thousands of them stood there. / But seeing the firmly barred door-leaves, Kṛṣṇa effortlessly,
the valiant one, struck them with his foot alone and brought them down. / Those two [doors] fell broken right where the army was arranged.
All those stationed there were slain, their limbs and necks crushed. / Then, entering the palace facing Kaṃsa, the two mighty ones,
swinging the two stout tusks, eager for combat, O fortunate one, / the two great-souled ones saw the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Seeing Govinda and the mighty Rāma, / fear entered Kaṃsa, and he then said to Cāṇūra, the best of wrestlers:
Kaṃsa said: / "On this occasion, O wrestler, slay the two cowherd boys! / Having divided my kingdom, I will effortlessly give you half of it."
Īśvara said: / On that occasion, Kṛṣṇa appeared to the two wrestlers as a great [adversary], / in the midst of the battle like another Great Meru in a forest;
in Kaṃsa's view, Acyuta was like the fire of cosmic dissolution; / to the women, he was Love incarnate; to his parents, like another child;
to the thirty gods, he was like Hari; to the cowherds, like a companion. / Thus in many forms they saw Hari, who is present everywhere.
Vasudeva, Akrūra, and the noble Nandagopa, / climbing onto another palace, watched that great slaughter.
Surrounded by the women of the inner apartments, the auspicious Devakī stood there, / her eyes filled with tears, gazing upon the face of her son.
Consoled by them, the lady went into another chamber. / Then all the hosts of gods, seated in their celestial chariots in the sky,
praised the lotus-eyed Acyuta with cries of victory. / "Slay Kaṃsa!" shouted the gods and the hosts of Maruts aloud.
Meanwhile, amid the reverberating blare of musical instruments, / the two mighty lions among the Yadus approached the two great wrestlers.
Govinda fought with Cāṇūra, and the plow-armed one with Muṣṭika; / the two great-souled ones fought, resembling dark and white mountains,
according to the rules of wrestling, with fists and blows of their feet. / A terrible slaughter took place, bringing fear even to the gods.
Then, having played with Cāṇūra for a long time, Janārdana / crushed the wrestler's limbs and threw him down with ease.
Vomiting much blood, he fell onto the surface of the earth; / and that great wrestler, who had caused grief to gods and Dānavas, died.
Likewise, Rāma fought for a long time with Muṣṭika; / the mighty one struck him on the chest with his fists.
With his bones and sinews shattered, he fell onto the surface of the earth; / then all the wrestlers fled upon seeing that prowess.
Deep, intense fear overcame Kaṃsa, who was afflicted with pain. / In the meantime, the two invincible heroes, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
those high-souled ones, climbed the lofty palace platform. / Striking Kaṃsa on the head with his palm alone, Janārdana,
Hari, hurled him down to the surface of the earth from the top of the palace. / With all his limbs shattered, he gave up his life on the earth.
When Kaṃsa was slain by Kṛṣṇa, Rāma of very great strength / also struck down his younger brother, named Sunāman, with his fist alone.
The supporter of the earth hurled that younger brother onto the earth. / Having slain the evil-minded Kaṃsa along with his younger brother, Rāma and Keśava,
approached their parents and bowed down with devotion. / Devakī and Vasudeva embraced them again and again,
and smelling their heads with affection, they longed tenderly for their sons; / Devakī’s breasts showered milk over the two of them.
Then, having comforted their parents, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa went outside. / In the meantime, divine celestial drums sounded in the sky,
and the lords of the gods rained down showers of flowers. / Having praised Janārdana with the divine hosts of Maruts and bowed to him,
they attained supreme joy and departed to their respective worlds. / Having bowed to the cowherd Nanda and to the elderly cowherds, Keśava,
righteous-minded, joyfully embraced [Nanda] along with Rāma; / Janārdana affectionately gave him much wealth and jewels.
Keśava honored all those elderly cowherds with garments, ornaments, and the like, / and with abundant riches and grain.
Dismissed by that Kṛṣṇa, those [cowherds], led by the cowherd Nanda, / departed for the divine cowpen, filled with joy and sorrow.
Approaching their maternal grandfather, the invincible Rāma and Kṛṣṇa / freed him from bondage and repeatedly comforted him.
Madhusūdana consecrated him in that kingdom, / and caused Kaṃsa’s post-funeral rites to be performed by the best of the twice-born.
Having installed the foremost Yadus, headed by Akrūra, in the kingdom, / and having made Ugrasena king, righteous Hari, the son of Vasudeva, / protected the earth according to dharma.

6.246.m: Śrī Maheśvara said: / Then Ānakadundubhi performed the sacred thread ceremony / of his two sons, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, according to the Vedic rite.
Rāma and Keśava were consecrated by the preceptor Garga, / by learned, divine Vaiṣṇavas, with pure and auspicious ablutions.
Having undergone the initiatory rites, the mighty Rāma and Kṛṣṇa / went to the house of Sāndīpani and bowed to the high-souled one.
Having studied the Vedas and Śāstras from that foremost of the twice-born, / they brought back his dead son and gave him as his teacher’s fee.
Having received words of blessing from that high-souled teacher, / those two bulls of the Yadus bowed to him and went to Mathurā.
Then, hearing that the invincible Kaṃsa had been killed by Kṛṣṇa, / that king’s father-in-law, the mighty Jarāsandha,
arrived with armies of thousands of akṣauhiṇīs of great might / and besieged the city of Mathurā to kill Kṛṣṇa.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, possessing great heroism, marched out from the excellent city / and saw that flood of forces crowded with elephants and horses.
Then Vāsudeva remembered his eternal, former form. / At the mere thought of him, Dāruka, Viṣṇu's charioteer,
brought the great eternal chariot named Sugrīvapuṣpaka, / drawn by divine steeds headed by Puṣpaka,
equipped with divine weapons—the conch, discus, mace, and others— / adorned with the banner of Garuḍa, invincible to the gods.
Reaching the earth and bowing to Govinda, Hari’s charioteer / presented the radiant chariot, equipped with weapons and horses.
Seeing it with joy, Kṛṣṇa circled the great chariot / and mounted it along with his elder brother, praised by hosts of Maruts.
Assuming a four-armed body, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, / wearing a diadem, earrings, and a garland, he set out towards the battle.
Valiant Baladeva too, taking his pestle and plow, / began to slay that army like a second Maheśvara.
And Dāruka swiftly drove the chariot in that battle, / like the wind driving fire in a forest overgrown with grass, bushes, and creepers.
Then the soldiers of Jarāsandha covered that chariot / with maces, iron bludgeons, spears, and clubs.
With his discus alone, Hari quickly cleaved them with ease, / as a great fire consumes abundant grass and wood with its flame.
Then, taking up the bow Śārṅga, with inexhaustible, sharp arrows / he cut down those armies so that nothing remained discernible.
In that great battle, some mighty warriors had their lotus faces severed by the discus; / some were crushed by the mace; some by other weapons;
some were cleaved by the sword; likewise others were pierced by arrows; / some had their necks struck by the plowshare, their heads smashed by the pestle.
Having slain that entire army in an instant, Madhusūdana, / the best of the Yadus, blew his conch, whose sound resembled the thunderbolt of dissolution.
Their hearts shattered by the blare of the conch, those mighty / warriors, along with their horses and elephants, fell down dead.
Indeed, that entire army of a thousand akṣauhiṇīs, / with horses, chariots, and elephants, was wiped out by Kṛṣṇa alone.
It was slain within half a prahara by Vāsudeva wielding Śārṅga. / Then all the hosts of gods, their minds filled with joy,
rained showers of flowers and cried, 'Well done! Well done!' / Having removed all the burden of the earth, the upholder of the earth
shone at the head of the battle, being praised by the gods. / Seeing his army destroyed, the exceedingly valiant Jarāsandha,
foolish-minded, quickly advanced to fight with Baladeva; / a terrible battle ensued between those two who never turned back in fights.
Rāma took up his plow, brought down Jarāsandha’s chariot along with its charioteer / in the battle, and the hero seized that mighty warrior.
Raising his pestle, he swiftly began to slay him. / Seeing the foremost of kings, Jarāsandha, brought to peril of his life
by mighty Rāma, like a great elephant by a lion, / the lord Kṛṣṇa said to his elder brother, 'He is not to be killed.'
The righteous-minded, wise one caused Jarāsandha to be released. / Releasing the enemy at Kṛṣṇa's word, the imperishable Saṃkarṣaṇa,
mounted the chariot with his younger brother and entered Mathurā. / Having encountered Kālayavana, who possessed great heroism and strength,
He told of the prowess of Vasudeva's two sons, / the slaying of the Dānavas, and likewise the death of Kaṃsa,
and the destruction of the akṣauhiṇī armies, as well as his own defeat; / he reported all of Kṛṣṇa's great deeds.
Hearing that, the furious Yavana, endowed with great might and prowess, / surrounded by thousands of crores of intoxicated Mlecchas,
the exceedingly powerful one, to aid that ruler of Magadha, / quickly marched with him to the city of Mathurā.
Covering the earth and its various provinces with his forces, / encamping his vast army, he laid siege to the city of Mathurā.
Kṛṣṇa, then thinking of the welfare of the city's inhabitants, / begged the ocean for land for the people to dwell upon.
The ocean gave Kṛṣṇa [a tract] thirty yojanas wide; / in the midst of the waters there he created the city of Dvāravatī,
endowed with many mansions, with golden walls and gateways, / enclosed by rows of divine houses made of diverse jewels,
and filled with delightful gardens and numerous ponds; / the lotus-eyed one created it like Amarāvatī of Indra.
Then, lifting up the citizens who were asleep in Mathurā, / Janārdana swiftly settled them at night in Dvārāvatī.
Awakening with their wives and sons, all those people, / seated upon the floors of golden palaces, attained the greatest astonishment,
surrounded by principal houses filled to abundance, as it were, / with abundant money and grain, divine garments, and ornaments.
Rejoicing in it, they dwelt like hosts of gods in heaven. / Then, to fight with the Yavana, the two exceedingly powerful ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
the masters of their own selves, marched outside of Mathurā. / Then Rāma, the great car-warrior, taking up his plow and pestle,
in fury struck down the great army of the Yavanas in battle. / Kṛṣṇa, stringing his bow Śārṅga, with arrows like flames of fire,
the son of Devakī burned up the entire army of the Mlecchas. / Seeing his army destroyed, the powerful Kālayavana,
the king of the Yavanas, fought with Vasudeva's son with a mace. / Kṛṣṇa too, having made slaughter with him for a long time, unaffected,
the lotus-eyed one turned away and ran from that battle. / He was pursued in great haste by the other, shouting, "Halt, halt!"
In haste the wise Kṛṣṇa entered a mountain cave. / There was sleeping King Mucukunda, the great sage.
The blessed Lord Hari stood invisible to that king. / The Yavana, a mighty hero, raised his mace in his hand
and entered that cave, having set out to slay Kṛṣṇa. / Seeing the sleeping king and mistaking him for Kṛṣṇa Janārdana,
he struck the great sage Mucukunda with his foot. / Then the venerable Mucukunda, the great sage, awakened,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, and he uttered the roar "huṃ!" / By the sound of his roar "huṃ!" and the glare of his anger,
the Yavana was burnt to ashes and gave up his life. / Then Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared before the royal sage,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes resembling lotuses, / holding a conch, discus, and mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments—Janārdana.
Seeing him of boundless splendor, the royal sage quickly arose; / the great sage said, "Oh, what good fortune! Oh, what good fortune!"
His whole body covered in horripilation, overwhelmed with joyful tears, / praising him with cries of victory, he bowed again and again.
Mucukunda said: / "Blessed am I, my purpose fulfilled, from seeing you, O Supreme Lord! / Today my birth has borne fruit; my life has borne fruit.
Homage to you, Vāsudeva, Lord of the world, wielder of the bow Śārṅga, / to Dāmodara, the divine one, the reservoir of splendors, homage!
Homage to Adhokṣaja, to Hari, to him who has the body of a man-lion; / homage to you, Rāghava, and lotus-eyed one!
Homage to Acyuta, the changeless, and to you, Ananta; / homage to you, Govinda, to Viṣṇu, to the victorious one, homage!
To Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, / to Mukunda, homage to you, to the fourfold manifestation!
Homage to the supremely auspicious one; homage to you, the Supreme Self, / to Vāsudeva, the peaceful one, to the Lord of the Yadus, homage!"
Maheśvara said: / Having thus praised Govinda, he bowed again and again. / Pleased, the Blessed Lord said to the great sage Mucukunda:
The Blessed Lord said: / "Choose a boon, O royal sage, whatever is in your heart." / Maheśvara said: / Then he too asked for liberation, free from return.
Then Kṛṣṇa gave him the divine, eternal world. / The wise king, abandoning his human form,
assuming a form equal to that of the divine Supreme Self, / mounted Garuḍa and entered the everlasting state.

6.247.m: Rudra said: / Having thus slain the Yavana there by means of the wise Mucukunda / and having given him the boon of liberation, the joy of the Yadus departed.
Hearing that the Yavana had been slain, the exceedingly wicked Jarāsaṃdha / fought with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by his own army.
Kṛṣṇa struck down that evil-minded one's entire army; / the king of Magadha fell swooning onto the surface of the earth.
Regaining consciousness after a long time, his limbs agitated, distressed by fear, / the lord of Magadha was unable to fight in battle with Rāma.
Turning away, followed by the remnant of his slain army, he fled swiftly, / considering the two exceedingly powerful ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, to be unconquerable.
Abandoning enmity toward the two of them, he entered his own city. / Then those two sons of Vasudeva, together with their army,
abandoned the city of Mathurā and entered the city of Dvārikā. / Dispatched by Indra, the Wind gave the assembly hall of the gods
to Kṛṣṇa with affection, built by Viśvakarman, / fashioned of diamonds and cat's-eye gems, adorned with many seats,
and resplendent with various jewel-encrusted, divine golden parasols. / Having obtained that delightful hall, Ugrasena and other kings
rejoiced together with the citizens, like the hosts of gods in heaven. / A king named Raivata, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku,
with affection gave his own daughter, a maiden endowed with all auspicious marks, / named Revatī by name, to Rāma.
Rāma married that Revatī according to the prescribed rules, / and delighted in her like the lord of the gods with Śacī.
There was a virtuous king of Vidarbha, righteous, named Bhīṣmaka; / he had auspicious sons, Rukma and the others.
Their younger sister was the fair-complexioned girl Rukmiṇī, / born from a portion of Kamalā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
In the state of Rāghava she was Sītā; in Kṛṣṇa's birth, she was Rukmiṇī; / in other incarnations as well, she is the companion of Viṣṇu.
Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa were born again in the Dvāpara age, / possessing the names Śiśupāla and Dantavaktra.
Born in the lineage of Cedi, endowed with great strength and prowess, / his son wished to give Rukmiṇī to Śiśupāla.
She of fair countenance did not desire Śiśupāla as her husband, however; / devoted to Viṣṇu from childhood, she was firm in her vows.
Dedicaing it to Kṛṣṇa as her husband, the maiden Rukmiṇī / always performed worship of the gods and gave various gifts.
Intent on the practice of vows and meditating on Puruṣottama, / the lord of her self and her husband, she dwelt in her father's palace.
To arrange her marriage to Śiśupāla, the best of kings, / along with his wise son Rukmin, made an effort.
Rukmiṇī sent a brāhmaṇa, the son of the family priest; / dedicated to Kṛṣṇa her husband, he swiftly went to Dvārakā.
Meeting Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and duly honored by both of them, / he related in private everything that Rukmiṇī had spoken.
Having heard that from the wise brāhmaṇa, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the lords, / [mounted] a sky-faring chariot filled with all weapons and missiles,
which was mounted with the great-souled Dāruka as chief charioteer, / and the two best of men swiftly went to the city of Vidarbha.
Kings from all realms had arrived to witness the marriage / of the wise Śiśupāla, led by Jarāsaṃdha.
At that time of the wedding, Rukmiṇī, adorned with gold ornaments, / went out outside the city with her female friends to worship Durgā.
At that very time, the son of Devakī arrived; / and the mighty Madhusūdana seized her as she stood in the chariot.
Quickly placing her on his chariot, he departed swiftly for his own abode. / Then, overcome with rage, the kings headed by Jarāsaṃdha,
along with prince Rukmin, stepped forth for battle; / enraged, accompanied by fourfold armies, they pursued Hari.
Mighty-armed Balabhadra, descending from the excellent chariot, / took his plow and pestle and struck down the foes in an instant.
