Chariots, horses, great elephants, and foot-soldiers / he forcefully struck down in battle with his plow and pestle.
By the fall of his plow, rows of chariots were crushed to dust, / and elephants fell to the ground like mountains struck by a thunderbolt.
Their heads split open, vomiting abundant blood, / the army was then destroyed in an instant by Balarāma alone,
with its horses, elephants, chariots, and foot-soldiers in the great battle; / on all sides of the field of battle flowed rivers of blood.
Broken, all the kings fled, afflicted with fear. / The mighty Rukmin, under the sway of wrath, waged slaughter against Kṛṣṇa.
Raising his bow, he struck the wielder of the Śārṅga with streams of arrows. / Then Govinda, laughing, effortlessly took up the Śārṅga bow,
and with a single arrow struck his chariot horses and his charioteer; / the supporter of the earth cut down his chariot, standard, and banner.
Carless, taking up a sword, he stood upon the ground; / but the heroic Kṛṣṇa shattered his sword with a single arrow.
Then, raising his fist, he struck Kṛṣṇa upon the chest; / Hari seized that hero in battle and bound him tightly.
Taking a sharp razor-headed arrow, Madhusūdana, laughing, / shaved his head and then released him, O Janārdana.
Overwhelmed with grief, hissing like a serpent, / he entered his own city and dwelt there indeed.

6.248.m: Rudra said: / Then Kṛṣṇa, with Rāma, Rukmiṇī, and Dāruka, / mounting his celestial chariot, went quickly to his own home.
Then, having entered the city of Dvārakā, the son of Devakī, / on an auspicious day and auspicious astrological moment, Hari, according to Vedic rites,
married the king's daughter, Rukmiṇī, adorned with gold. / At that time of the wedding, divine drums sounded in the sky,
and the best of the gods rained down showers of flowers. / Vasudeva and Ugrasena, as well as Akrūra, the best of the Yadus,
Balabhadra of great splendor, and whatever other eminent Yadus there were, / conducted the marriage of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī in great happiness.
Then the cowherd Nanda arrived with cowherds and flocks of herdsmen, / and Yaśodā came with well-adorned women.
All the wives of Vasudeva, headed by Devakī, / goddess Revatī, Rohiṇī, and other women of the city,
performed all the wedding rites, filled with joy. / The worship of the gods to be performed with love there Devakī
performed according to rule, together with the elderly royal women; / every marital rite was indeed a festive celebration with the best of the twice-born.
She fed the brāhmaṇas and presented auspicious garments and ornaments; / Ugrasena and the other kings there were also well honored.
The cowherds headed by Nanda, and the women headed by Yaśodā, / with much gold, jewels, and garments with ornaments
were honored, and they were greatly delighted at that great wedding festival. / Embracing the wedded pair, they bowed to Agni.
Greeted with blessings by foremost brāhmaṇas knowing the Veda, / bride and groom shone upon that wedding altar.
Then to the brāhmaṇas, the elders, and the royal princes, along with his wife, / the son of Devakī bowed, and also to his elder brother.
Having thus completed all the wedding rites, Madhusūdana / sent off all the kings who had assembled there.
Honored there by Hari, the foremost kings departed; / the greatly noble brāhmaṇas went to their own dwellings.
Together with Rukmiṇī, the righteous, imperishable son of Devakī / dwelt in great happiness upon the splendid roof of the celestial palace.
With her he took delight, just as Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, / being praised by sages and by host of gods in heaven.
Day after day, cheerful in spirit, Janārdana in comfort / dwelt, the eternal one, in radiant Dvāravatī.

6.249.m: Śrī Rudra said: / The daughter of Satrājit, renowned by the name of Satyā, / born of a portion of the Earth, was another wife of Kṛṣṇa.
The daughter of the Sun, highly fortunate, known by the name of Kālindī, / was his third wife, appearing as an incarnation of Līlā.
Mitravindā of pure smile, daughter of Vinda and Anuvinda, / a maiden standing in her svayaṃvara, Janārdana married.
Having bound seven furious bulls with a single rope, / he whose eyes are broad as lotus petals took her as the prize for his valor.
Satrājit, the lord of the earth, gave the great jewel / named Syamantaka to his younger brother, the noble Prasena.
Once Madhusūdana asked for that excellent jewel; / Prasena then spoke forcefully to that Vāsudeva.
Prasena said: / 'This jewel brings forth eight loads of gold every day. / Therefore, this [gem] called Syamantaka must not be given by me to anyone.'
Mahādeva said: / But Kṛṣṇa, knowing his intention, remained silent. / Once, in order to hunt, Kṛṣṇa, along with all the foremost Yadus,
entered the great forest, accompanied by Prasena and other mighty men. / Followed by thousands, each went to slay wild beasts.
Prasena, all alone in the great forest, went far away. / A lion, coming upon him as he was seen, killed him and took the jewel.
The mighty Jāmbavat killed that lion, took the gem, / and quickly entered a cave frequented by celestial women.
When the sun had set, Vāsudeva with his followers, / having seen the moon risen on the fourth day, entered his own city.
Then all the citizens spoke among themselves of Kṛṣṇa: / 'Govinda, under the pretext of hunting in the forest, killed Prasena,
and took the excellent jewel Syamantaka without any fear.' / Hearing then what was spoken by the people of Dvārakā, Hari,
out of fear of ignorant folk, went into the dense forest with all the Yadus, / and showed them all [Prasena] slain in the forest by a lion.
Having obtained his own purification, stationing his great army right there, / he alone, bow and mace in hand, went into the dense forest.
Seeing a great cave, Kṛṣṇa entered without hesitation. / There, in a spotless dwelling illumined by various excellent gems,
a nurse, playfully putting the son of Jāmbavat into a cradle, / placing the gem at the head of the cradle, was rocking it and singing with joy:
'A lion killed Prasena, and the lion was killed by Jāmbavat. / Do not weep, delicate child; this Syamantaka is indeed yours!'
Hearing that, the valiant Vāsudeva blew his conch shell. / At that mighty sound, Jāmbavat came forth.
A terrible fight took place between the two, continuous for ten nights, / with fists like thunderbolts, causing terror to all creatures.
Perceiving Kṛṣṇa's increasing strength and the waning of his own strength, / and recalling the former words of the Supreme Self,
[he thought:] 'This is that Rāma descended here once more to protect dharma. / My Lord has come to grant my heart's desire!'
Knowing this, the lord of bears ceased that combat, / and with folded hands said to Govinda in great astonishment, 'Who are you?'
Ceasing the fight, Śauri spoke with a deep voice: / The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said: 'I am the son of Vasudeva, called Vāsudeva.
You have taken my jewel named Syamantaka without any fear. / Let it be given to me quickly, or you will meet your death!'
Mahādeva said: / Hearing that, Jāmbavat, delighted, prostrated himself like a staff. / Circumambulating and bowing down, he humbly addressed Keśava:
Jāmbavat said: / 'I am blessed, I have achieved my purpose by the sight of you, O Lord! / I am your servant from my former existence, O son of Devakī!
You have granted, O Govinda, the combat long desired. / This fight which was waged by me out of delusion with you, my master— / forgive it, O Lord of the World, eternal ocean of compassion!'
Mahādeva said: / Having spoken thus, bowing down and paying homage again and again, / seating the Lord humbly on a seat made of various jewels,
washing his feet that resembled autumn lotuses with auspicious water, / and worshipping the chief of Yadus with the madhuparka rite,
having worshipped him according to rule with garments and celestial ornaments, / [he gave] his daughter named Jāmbavatī, a maiden endowed with charm.
He gave that jewel of a maiden to him of boundless splendour to be his wife, / and along with other chief gems, he gave the gem named Syamantaka.
Marrying that maiden right there, Hari, slayer of enemy heroes, delighted, / granted highest liberation to Jāmbavat with affection.
Taking his daughter, the maiden Jāmbavatī, with joy, / coming out of that cave, he went to the city of Dvārakā.
The best of Yadus gave the jewel called Syamantaka to Satrājit; / and he too gave that excellent gem to his own daughter, the maiden.
Looking at the moon on the fourth [tithi] of the bright half of the month of Bhādrapada / brings false accusation, so they say; therefore, one should avoid it.
If a man happens to see the cool-rayed [moon] on that fourth [tithi], / hearing the story of Syamantaka, he is freed from false accusation.
Sulakṣmaṇā, Nāgnajitī, and the renowned Suśīlā— / these three fair-faced maidens were daughters of the king of Madra.
Radiant, present at their svayaṃvara, they chose Kṛṣṇa; / and on a single day, the best of Yadus wedded them.
There were eight principal queens of that great soul, Rukmiṇī and the rest: / Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and pure-smiling Kālindī,
Mitravindā, Jāmbavatī, Nāgnajitī, Sulakṣmaṇā, / and the slender-limbed queen named Suśīlā is remembered as the eighth.
There was a rākṣasa named Naraka, born of the Earth, of great heroism, / who conquered Śakra, lord of the gods, and indeed all the gods in battle.
He took by force the two radiant earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, / and various jewels belonging to the gods,
Airāvata belonging to Mahendra, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas, / the rubies and other treasures of the lord of wealth, along with the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures.
That son of the Earth carried off women and apsarases, / and seizing by force the weapons of those dwellers of heaven, such as the thunderbolt,
he slew gods with those very weapons; and dwelling in the sky, / he lived in a celestial assembly-hall built by Maya, in a city in the clear heavens.
Then all the hosts of gods, putting the husband of Śacī at their head, / afflicted by fear, sought refuge with Kṛṣṇa, of untroubled deeds.
Kṛṣṇa too, hearing of all that conduct of Naraka, / granted fearlessness to the gods and thought of the son of Vinatā.
At that moment, that mighty son of Vinatā stood before Hari / with folded hands, worshipped by all the gods.
Mounting that best of birds, Keśava, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, / praised by sages, set out for the dwelling of the rākṣasa.
Blazing in the sky like the orb of the sun, / filled with many rākṣasas and furnished with celestial ornaments,
Kṛṣṇa saw that city, impenetrable even to the gods. / Looking upon its enclosures, the valiant Lord, with his disc,
cut them through with dazzling splendour, like the sun cutting through darkness. / Then all those rākṣasas by hundreds and by thousands,
raising their tridents, advanced face-to-face for battle. / Then with celestial javelins, bhiṇḍipālas, and sharp spears,
they struck Keśava, as straw [strikes] fire. / Thereupon, taking up the Śārṅga bow, the Lord whose emblem is Garuḍa
severed their celestial weapons with arrows resembling tongues of flame, / and the powerful Supreme Person severed with his disc
the necks of those [warriors], their elephants, and swift horses. / Some were cut to pieces by his disc, others struck down by his arrows,
and some rākṣasas were slain by his mace on that field of battle. / In this manner all those rākṣasas were felled to the surface of the earth.
like mountains shattered by the thunderbolt hurled by Indra. / Having slain all the Dānavas, the lotus-eyed Lord,
the Supreme Person, blew the great conch Pāñcajanya. / Then that powerful Daitya Naraka took up his bow,
mounted a divine chariot, and went out to fight Keśava. / Between the two of them a terrible, tumultuous, hair-raising battle took place,
with thousands of arrows, like two clouds pouring rain. / Then eternal Vāsudeva, with a crescent-shaped arrow,
valiant, cut the bow of that chief of Rākṣasas. / He hurled a great divine weapon into Naraka's broad chest.
With his heart pierced by it, the great Asura fell upon the earth, / roaring like a great mountain shattered by Indra's thunderbolt.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having approached the vicinity of that Rākṣasa, / prayed to by the Earth, said to the Rākṣasa: 'Choose a boon.' / And that Rākṣasa said to Kṛṣṇa, who was seated upon Garuḍa:
'I have no need of a boon; I am Naraka, yet still / for the sake of the welfare of other worlds I choose an excellent boon.
On the day of my death, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of all beings, / when people take an auspicious bath, O Madhusūdana, / let them not attain hell! May it be thus, O Dispeller of fear!'
Mahādeva said: / 'So be it,' said Govinda, and the Lord granted him the boon. / Then, looking directly upon Hari's feet, resembling autumn lotuses,
resplendent with anklets of diamonds and cat's-eye gems, / worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others, by the gods and by sages,
the son of the Earth gave up his life-breaths and attained resemblance to the form of Hari. / Then all the hosts of gods, their minds filled with joy,
showered rains of flowers, and the great sages praised him. / Entering his city, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa
[took back] the jewels of the inhabitants of heaven seized by him by force, / and the earrings of the mother of the gods, and likewise the horse Uccaiḥśravas,
Airāvata, the best of elephants, and the glowing jeweled mountain. / All this the best of Yadus gave to Indra, bearer of the thunderbolt.
Having conquered kings from every realm, that mighty Naraka / had then abducted sixteen thousand maidens.
All of them, kept captive in Naraka's inner quarters at that time, / upon seeing Kṛṣṇa of great valor, resembling a hundred gods of love,
chose him as their husband, the Lord of all, who pervades everything. / At that very time Govinda, who possesses infinite forms,
took their hands in marriage according to the sacred rule, the Supreme Person. / Then all the sons of Naraka, placing the Earth in front,
went for refuge to Govinda; and he, an ocean of compassion, protected them. / Establishing them all in that kingdom out of respect for the Earth's word,
and mounting all those noble women onto Indra's celestial chariot, / he had them escorted to Dvāravatī by the illustrious divine messengers.
Mounting the son of Vinatā together with Satyā, Keśava / went swiftly to heaven to see the mother of the gods.
Entering that city of the king of gods, Janārdana / of mighty strength descended from the best of birds together with his wife,
and there paid homage to the mother, who is venerable to the inhabitants of heaven. / Aditi, affectionate toward her son, embraced him with her arms,
seated him on an excellent seat, and worshipped him with devotion. / The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, headed by Śatakratu,
duly worshipped the Supreme Lord there. / Having come to the house of Śacī, the renowned Satyabhāmā
was welcomed by the goddess and seated on a comfortable seat. / At that time the attendants brought beautiful flowers of the pārijāta tree
and out of affection gave them to the goddess Śacī, as commanded by the thousand-eyed Indra. / Taking those flowers, the slender-waisted goddess Śacī
bound them in the dark, spotless hair upon her head. / Showing disrespect there to the renowned Satyabhāmā,
thinking, 'This mortal woman does not deserve the auspicious flower fit for gods,' / she did not give any flowers to her.
Going out from that city, filled with anger, / Satyā, the lotus-eyed, approached her husband Kṛṣṇa and said:
Satyā said: / 'This Śacī, O best of Yadus, has become arrogant on account of the pārijāta; / without giving any to me, O Govinda, she bound them upon her own head.'
Mahādeva said: / Hearing what was spoken by Satyā, Vāsudeva of mighty strength / uprooted the pārijāta tree, placed it upon Garuḍa,
swiftly mounted the mighty son of Vinatā together with Satyā, / and the son of Devakī set out for the charming city of Dvārakā.
Then Śatakratu, the king of gods, overcome with anger, / together with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Sādhyas, and hosts of the Maruts,
mounted Airāvata and went to fight against Keśava. / Then all the hosts of gods, surrounding Janārdana,
poured showers of weapons, like clouds upon a great mountain. / Kṛṣṇa cut to pieces those weapons of the celestial gods with his discus.
The mighty son of Vinatā, enraged, by the striking of his wings / knocked down those gods just as wind scatters straw.
Then the thousand-eyed Indra, the lord and ruler of the gods, angered, / suddenly released his blazing thunderbolt, wishing to slay Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa caught that thunderbolt playfully with a single hand. / Then the thousand-eyed Indra, frightened, descended from the king of elephants,
stood before him with folded palms, bowed down to Janārdana, / and, having praised him with hymns of praise, spoke with a faltering voice:
Indra said: / 'This pārijāta, fit for gods, O Kṛṣṇa, was given by you long ago / to me and to the gods; how can it remain among mortals?'
Mahādeva said: / Then the Blessed Lord spoke to the thousand-eyed Indra standing before him: / 'Satyā was disrespected by Śacī in your house, O Lord of the gods.
Without giving any pārijāta flowers to Satyā, that daughter of Puloman, / your beloved, wore them on her own head.
For her sake, O Lord of gods, the pārijāta was taken by me; / I promised to give it to her, O Lord of the hosts of gods,
saying: "I shall establish the pārijāta in your house, O Vāsava." / Therefore, the pārijāta is not to be given back today, O Lord of the gods.
For the benefit of the gods I will bring it to the surface of the earth. / For that long, O Lord of gods, let the pārijāta remain in my abode.
When I have gone to heaven, O Śakra, take it as you wish.' / Mahādeva said: / Having spoken thus, the best of Yadus himself gave him back the thunderbolt.
Saying 'So be it,' the thunderbolt-bearer bowed down to Govinda / and departed for his divine city, surrounded by the hosts of gods.
Kṛṣṇa too, seated upon Garuḍa together with Queen Satyā, / praised by sages, entered Dvāravatī.
Placing the pārijāta, the tree of the gods, near Satyā, / all-pervading Hari delighted all of his wives.
During the nights, Madhusūdana, the glorious one, who assumes the universal form / and bestows happiness, dwelt in the houses of all of them.
